title: Universal Basic Income
resolution: Resolved: The United States federal government should provide a universal basic income.
summary: A universal basic income would give every adult a regular cash payment with no conditions. Pilot programs have tested smaller versions. Would a national program be wise?

background.p: A **universal basic income** (UBI) is a regular cash payment to every adult, regardless of income or work, with no rules on how it's spent. Most U.S. experiments have tested **guaranteed income**: payments to selected low- or moderate-income people, which is narrower than a true UBI.

In Stockton, California, 125 residents received $500 a month for two years (2019–2021). Recipients moved from part-time to full-time work at more than twice the rate of a comparison group and reported better well-being. A larger randomized study run by OpenResearch gave $1,000 a month for three years; recipients worked about 1.3 fewer hours a week than the comparison group, spent the money mostly on basic needs, and early gains in stress and mental health faded. The researchers called the results mixed.

Cost is a central question. Because a UBI goes to everyone, even a modest payment adds up to trillions of dollars a year, unless it replaces other programs or is paid for by large tax changes. Supporters and critics disagree about which programs it should replace.

positions: Some pilots (such as Stockton) found no drop, or even more full-time work, among recipients.
The larger OpenResearch study found a modest drop of about 1.3 hours a week, and critics argue a permanent national program could have larger effects.

terms.def: Regular cash for everyone, with no conditions.
Cash payments to people below an income level, often in pilot programs.
Available only to people with incomes below a set limit.
A plan in which people below an income level receive money from the tax system instead of paying.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A basic income would give everyone a secure floor, simply and with dignity.

args.claim: Cash gives people security and freedom to improve their lives.
args.warrant: A steady floor lets people handle emergencies, look for better jobs, train for new careers or care for family without falling into crisis.
args.evidence: Stockton SEED results (more full-time work, more people able to cover a $400 emergency); guaranteed-income pilot reports.
args.response: The negative answers that Stockton was small, and the larger OpenResearch study found mixed results, including slightly less work.

args.claim: A universal program is simpler and less stigmatizing.
args.warrant: Means-tested programs require paperwork, and many eligible people never receive benefits. Giving everyone the same payment removes red tape and shame.
args.evidence: Research on take-up rates in existing programs; administrative costs of means-tested aid.
args.response: The negative replies that sending money to the wealthy is wasteful; it raises the cost enormously for little gain.

args.claim: It removes traps in current programs.
args.warrant: When benefits shrink as earnings rise, some people lose almost as much aid as they gain in pay. A universal payment doesn't shrink when you work more.
args.evidence: Analyses of effective marginal tax rates for low-income families; economists' work on the negative income tax.
args.response: The negative argues those traps can be fixed by phasing benefits out more slowly, at far less cost.

args.warrant: People know their own needs best; studies show they spend cash mostly on necessities rather than on harmful things.
args.evidence: OpenResearch study findings on spending (food, housing, transportation); Stockton spending data.
args.response: The negative answers that responsible spending doesn't settle whether a national program is affordable or the best use of the money.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: A universal basic income would cost too much, could reduce work, and spreads money too thinly.

args.warrant: Paying even a modest amount to every adult costs trillions each year, requiring large tax increases or cuts to programs people rely on.
args.evidence: Budget arithmetic using Census population counts; analyses of UBI proposals by budget groups.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the net cost is smaller once taxes recover payments from higher earners and some programs are replaced.

args.claim: It may reduce work over time.
args.warrant: When people receive income regardless of work, some will work less; across a whole economy, that lowers output and tax revenue.
args.evidence: OpenResearch results (about 1.3 fewer hours a week); earlier U.S. negative income tax experiments in the 1970s.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the drop was modest and some time went to caregiving, education or job searching.

args.claim: Targeted programs help the poor more per dollar.
args.warrant: Money given to everyone is money not concentrated on those in greatest need; targeted aid can give poor families much more for the same budget.
args.evidence: Comparisons of targeted versus universal transfer costs; research on the EITC and child tax credits.
args.response: The affirmative argues targeting misses many eligible people, and universal programs build broad public support.

args.claim: The evidence doesn't yet support a national program.
args.warrant: Pilots are small, temporary and local; a permanent national program could change prices, work and behavior in ways pilots can't show.
args.evidence: The researchers' own description of the OpenResearch results as mixed; the small size of Stockton's study.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the evidence so far shows few harms, and a national program can be phased in and studied.

strawmen.strawman: UBI supporters want people to get paid to sit on the couch.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue cash gives security to work, train or care for family, and pilots found little drop in work.
strawmen.steelman: A universal floor gives everyone security and freedom, avoids the red tape and work traps of current programs, and pilots show people spend it on necessities.

strawmen.strawman: UBI opponents don't care about poor people.
strawmen.why: Many opponents favor targeted aid that gives the poor more per dollar.
strawmen.steelman: A universal payment would cost trillions, may reduce work, and spreads money to everyone instead of concentrating it on those in need; pilots don't show a national program would work.

weak.why: No credible estimate supports this; argue about net cost and value instead.

weak.arg: People will spend it all on drugs and gambling.
weak.why: Studies found spending mostly on basic needs; the claim is contradicted by evidence.

aff: How much would you pay each adult, and what would it cost in a year?
Which existing programs would it replace?
What did the OpenResearch study find about hours worked?
neg: What did recipients in Stockton and the OpenResearch study spend money on?
What share of eligible people actually receive means-tested benefits?
Would you support a smaller guaranteed income for low-income families?
